title: Designing connection that ends with the moment
role: Product strategy, UX research, product design, prototyping & front-end development
introLead: PACEPOP is a temporary social layer for people sharing one real-world activity.
introSupport: It lets a small running group coordinate, ask for help and close the experience without exchanging contact information or creating a permanent group chat.
summary: A mobile experience for short-lived running groups, replacing permanent group chats and contact exchange with QR entry, temporary identities, safety-aware coordination and explicit room retention.
contribution: In a two-person team, I owned product strategy, UX research, product design, prototyping and front-end development. I translated the temporary-group premise into separate Host and Runner flows, designed the safety and privacy states, and built the interactive prototype used to test the end-to-end experience.
outcome: A working mobile prototype spanning two role-specific flows and 26 designed interface states. It demonstrates account-free entry, live group awareness, lightweight communication, help and exit states, and an explicit end to the room. The next validation step is field testing whether a temporary room reduces social overhead while preserving enough continuity for safety.
imageAlt: PACEPOP prototype screens showing QR entry, the live Runner map and the in-run Help response
visualCaption: 01 / Working prototype: temporary entry, live coordination and safety-aware support.

sections.title: A short encounter should not create a permanent social obligation
sections.lead: Small events create an immediate need to coordinate, but the usual tools ask for a longer relationship.
sections.body: People who meet through Luma events, running groups or one-night activities often need a shared place for directions, updates and safety. Creating a permanent group chat or exchanging contact information solves the moment by adding another channel to manage afterward. The social and privacy cost is larger than the brief connection requires.

comparison.observation: Temporary groups are pushed into permanent communication tools before they can coordinate.
comparison.response: Create a purpose-bound room that is easy to enter, useful during the activity and designed to end afterward.

sections.title: Let the life of the product match the life of the group
sections.lead: The group does not need a new social network. It needs a temporary layer of shared awareness.
sections.body: The product direction centered on four principles: join without an account, use a temporary identity, request only activity-specific access, and make retention visible. This reframed disappearance as a feature rather than a missing capability.

details.label: Entry
details.body: A single QR replaces account creation, friend requests and contact exchange.

details.label: Identity
details.body: A temporary nickname and avatar are enough for the group to recognize one another during the run.

details.label: Exit
details.body: The room has a visible retention window instead of becoming another permanent inbox.

sections.title: One scan opens two purpose-built experiences
sections.lead: Host and Runner share the same room, but they do not need the same interface.
sections.body: The Runner flow prioritizes location, pace, group distance and quick signals. The Host flow prioritizes the whole crew: who is ready, who is falling behind, which request is open and whether the group can safely finish. Separating these responsibilities kept each view focused while preserving one shared system state.

flow.label: Role-based journey

steps.label: Enter
steps.detail: Scan a QR, choose a temporary identity and grant only the permissions needed for the run.

steps.label: Coordinate
steps.detail: Runners send lightweight signals while the Host monitors position, spread and open alerts.

steps.label: Close
steps.detail: The group sees a shared result and the room follows an explicit retention window.

flow.caption: The same room state is translated into different decisions for the Host and Runner.

sections.title: Design the difficult moments before the celebratory ones
sections.lead: A runner who is moving cannot compose a careful message or decode a subtle notification.
sections.body: Large Help, Water, Rest and Give Up actions turn common running situations into fast, legible signals. Help keeps the runner's last known position visible and tells them that nearby people are checking. Give Up avoids failure language and keeps location available long enough to support a safe transition out of the run.

comparison.observation: Free-form chat is slow and ambiguous when someone is tired, separated from the group or needs assistance.
comparison.response: Use named states, strong visual contrast and clear follow-up language for time-sensitive coordination.

sections.title: End with recognition, then let the room disappear
sections.lead: Temporary does not have to feel disposable.
sections.body: Quick chat and KUDO create enough warmth for a shared activity without asking participants to become permanent contacts. At the end, the Host chooses how long results and chat remain available. The closure screen makes that decision explicit instead of hiding retention inside settings or policy copy.

details.label: During
details.body: Short preset messages reduce typing and keep communication tied to the run.

details.label: After
details.body: KUDO and a team summary provide a lightweight social ending.

details.label: Retention
details.body: The Host selects one hour, one day or one week for results and chat to remain available.

sections.title: Build the state system, not only the happy path
sections.lead: I carried the interaction model into a working front-end prototype.
sections.body: The prototype covers 13 Runner states and 13 Host states, including entry, permissions, live movement, temporary signals, help escalation, voluntary exit, roster controls, simulation and room closure. Building both sides exposed dependencies that a linear screen deck would miss: shared status language, permission timing, alert acknowledgement and retention behavior.

comparison.observation: A polished happy path cannot show whether two roles remain understandable when the group's state changes.
comparison.response: Prototype the operational states and transitions so the interaction logic can be exercised end to end.

content.caption: A temporary room begins without an account or phone number.
One QR replaces contact exchange and permanent group setup.
A lightweight identity is enough for one shared activity.
Permissions are explained in the context of the run.
Runner view keeps the group, pace and actions in one glance.
The Host defines the route before opening the room.
The lobby shows who joined and who is ready.
Water and rest become quick, named signals.
A separated runner can be located without opening chat.
Help confirms that the Host and crew are responding.
Leaving the run uses a clear, reversible confirmation.
Short messages keep conversation tied to the activity.
KUDO gives the group a lightweight social ending.
The personal finish state closes the run before results.
Team results preserve recognition without a permanent feed.
Host alerts translate group movement into actionable states.
The roster exposes status, distance and unresolved help.
A simulator exercises the system beyond the happy path.

source: User-confirmed two-person project scope and ownership; working PACEPOP prototype and product specification inspected September 2026. Prototype screenshots captured from the supplied local build.

title: From a nonprofit mission to a live website
role: Website team lead, UX/UI design, frontend & publishing
introLead: I carried a nonprofit website from audience needs through frontend delivery and publishing.
introSupport: The published experience connects families, schools, volunteers, donors and partners with clear paths into the foundation's mission.
summary: An end-to-end website project for a swim-education nonprofit, connecting a shared mission with clear paths for families, schools, volunteers, donors and partners.
contribution: I led the website team, owned the UX/UI design and HTML frontend implementation, and published the website. I collaborated with a backend developer on the surrounding program, outreach and reporting workflows.
outcome: A publicly accessible, responsive website at swimuphill.org, taken from UX/UI design through frontend implementation and publishing. Launch is the documented outcome; enrollment, donation and conversion improvements are not claimed without post-launch data.
imageAlt: Swim Up Hill published homepage with interactive location globe and program navigation
visualCaption: 01 / Published website, captured September 2026. Impact figures describe the foundation, not measured website results.

sections.title: One mission had to serve very different visitors
sections.body: Families, schools, volunteers and donors arrive with different questions. The UX challenge was to connect the foundation's story with a relevant next step for each audience, without making everyone navigate the same long explanation.

sections.title: Let visitors recognize their own path
sections.body: The homepage groups entry points by visitor type. A parent can move toward program options, a school toward a visit, and a supporter toward volunteering, giving or partnership. This organizes the experience around visitor intent rather than the nonprofit's internal departments.

comparison.observation: Different audiences need different information before they can act.
comparison.response: Explicit audience entry points, each paired with a relevant next action.

sections.title: Carry the design into
sections.lead: I carried the interface into HTML frontend implementation and publishing.
sections.body: The public experience includes program discovery, location exploration and mobile navigation, while collaboration with a backend developer connected the website work to broader operational needs.

sections.title: Own the handoff through publishing
sections.body: My responsibility did not end with a design file. I led the website work through implementation and public release. The live site is the primary artifact; the screenshots below capture the published experience rather than a speculative redesign.

content.caption: Published homepage: audience-specific paths connect visitors to relevant services and ways to participate.
Published program view reached from the Parent entry point. Capture of the public interface, not a completed enrollment transaction.
Published mobile experience with persistent bottom navigation.

title: Building product worlds with Blender MCP
status: Six Blender product and character renders
introLead: Blender MCP became an editable control layer for a product and character study.
introSupport: I directed editable modeling, materials, lighting and camera changes, then refined hierarchy through visual review.
summary: An AI-assisted 3D production study using Blender MCP to model a cosmetic bottle, build a restrained product stage and develop a companion mascot through lighting and composition iterations.
contribution: I used Blender MCP as a conversational control layer for modeling, material, lighting and camera changes, then reviewed every render visually and refined the hierarchy by hand. The case study uses the original high-resolution stills from my Drive archive.
outcome: A coherent six-image study spanning product close-ups, staged lighting variations and two character directions. The work demonstrates how I combine generative tooling with direct visual judgment rather than treating an AI output as the finished design.
imageAlt: Mint cosmetic bottle with a gold cap on a layered studio pedestal
visualCaption: Final product-lighting study from the original Blender MCP image set.

cover.annotation: Blender MCP / product and character studies

sections.title: Fast scene changes still needed a design point of view
sections.body: Conversational tooling could produce modeling, material and lighting changes quickly, but speed alone did not create a coherent visual system. The cosmetic bottle and mascot needed consistent proportions, color, surface contrast and staging across product and character directions.

sections.title: Use conversation as a control layer,
sections.lead: Blender MCP let me direct modeling, material, lighting and camera changes through conversation.
sections.body: I reviewed each result as a designer, then refined proportion, silhouette, contrast and framing from what the render actually showed rather than accepting the first generated pass.

flow.label: Blender MCP iteration loop

steps.label: Direct
steps.detail: Describe the form, material, light or camera change in visual terms.

steps.label: Build
steps.detail: Use Blender MCP to translate that direction into editable scene changes.

steps.label: Review
steps.detail: Inspect the rendered silhouette, hierarchy, surface response and composition.

steps.label: Refine
steps.detail: Tune the scene through another focused prompt or a direct adjustment in Blender.

flow.caption: Retrospective summary of the AI-assisted Blender workflow used for these studies.

sections.title: Build the product from readable proportions
sections.body: The product study starts with a recognizable bottle silhouette: a broad cylindrical body, a narrower neck, a reflective cap and a label band that remains legible from a distance. A stepped podium and circular backdrop give the form enough context without competing with it.

details.label: Silhouette
details.body: Simple stacked volumes keep the bottle recognizable across close and wide views.

details.label: Material contrast
details.body: A matte mint body, glossy label detail and warm metallic cap separate the main surfaces.

details.label: Stage
details.body: Soft peach forms and an elevated plinth create depth while preserving a product-first hierarchy.

sections.title: Tune hierarchy through four lighting studies
sections.body: The four product renders test different relationships between crop, camera distance, background exposure and directional light. Together they show how the same object can move from a graphic close-up to a bright catalog composition and then to a more atmospheric final stage.

sections.title: Carry the same softness into a mascot
sections.body: Two mascot variations extend the palette and rounded massing into character design. The large eyes, compact proportions and small pose or accessory changes make the figure more expressive while keeping it visually connected to the product world.

content.caption: Product study 01 / Close framing used to inspect the bottle silhouette, cap and label relationship.
Product study 02 / Wider composition introducing the layered plinth and circular backdrop.
Lighting study 03 / A stronger directional setup tests shadow, edge light and atmosphere.
Lighting study 04 / Balanced studio light keeps the product dominant while preserving depth in the stage.
Mascot study 01 / Rounded form, pastel surfaces and a restrained pose carry the product world's visual language into character design.
Mascot study 02 / A second expression and accessory variation tests personality without changing the core silhouette.

source: User-supplied Bubba's LA Drive archive, 10. personal project/0706_mcp/pictures, reviewed September 2026.

title: Turning a contact network into a daily next step
introLead: A contact database became a focused daily decision tool.
introSupport: Ranked signals, relevant capabilities and warm-introduction routes support one clear next action.
summary: A mobile-oriented decision-support dashboard for business development, connecting ranked signals, relevant capabilities and warm introduction routes to a clear daily priority.
contribution: I built the spreadsheet-to-dashboard workflow and its mobile HTML interface. I integrated an 11,571-contact professional network into the supporting workbook and refined the experience through stakeholder feedback, including clearer priorities and progress that survives a refresh.
outcome: A working mobile dashboard and documented July 2026 handoff. The interface is a read-only view of the workbook; daily contact and skip states are stored locally in the browser. It does not send messages or write changes back to the workbook. Screenshots use fictional data; no revenue or conversion lift is claimed.
imageAlt: Original Daily Target dashboard rendered with fictional example companies, scores and next actions
visualCaption: 01 / Original internship interface with fictional data. Real contacts, client relationships and outreach details have been excluded.

sections.title: Design around the decision, not the database
sections.body: The useful question was not how to display every contact. It was which opportunity to review next, why it mattered, and whether an introduction route existed. I brought the score, signal, capability fit, supporting context and next action into one focused view.

sections.title: Keep the workbook
sections.lead: The workbook owns the scoring rubric and network matching.
sections.body: The dashboard reads those results and presents a ranked queue with geography, signal-type and warm-route filters. It can load an updated workbook without creating a second, competing database.

comparison.observation: A rich spreadsheet is difficult to turn into a quick mobile decision.
comparison.response: A focused read-only view: today's priority, why it fits, the next action and a ranked queue.

sections.title: Protect progress from everyday interruptions
sections.body: Stakeholder feedback exposed two practical risks: a refresh could erase daily progress, and moving a spreadsheet column could break the data mapping. I added date-scoped local persistence for contact/skip states and header-based column resolution with explicit missing-field errors.

comparison.observation: Refreshing a mobile tab loses check-offs; fixed column positions make imports fragile.
comparison.response: Restore daily progress after reload and resolve fields by header name rather than position.

sections.title: Make ownership and limitations explicit
sections.body: The handoff documented the master workbook, scoring and matching logic, setup responsibilities and known limitations. Keeping the dashboard read-only simplified the interface and protected the workbook, but meant local check-offs were not a shared, cross-device record. Broader network coverage and company-owned automation remained follow-up work.

content.caption: Original ranked-queue interface with fictional data: compare priority, signal type and introduction route.
Original mobile interface after skipping a sample lead. Fictional companies and illustrative scores; no real outreach occurred.
